name: Ibadan Metropolis
description: The eleven LGAs forming greater Ibadan, once West Africa's largest city by area and Nigeria's colonial-era administrative and commercial capital of the west.

wikiNotes.title: 19th-century founding
wikiNotes.note: Ibadan was founded around 1829 as a war camp by Yoruba warriors from Oyo, Ife, and Ijebu, later growing into the largest Yoruba city.

wikiNotes.title: Colonial administrative capital
wikiNotes.note: Ibadan served as the capital of the old Western Region and later Oyo State, seeding much of Nigeria's early university, radio, and print-media infrastructure.

wikiNotes.title: Urban sprawl
wikiNotes.note: The five core 'Ibadan North/South' LGAs form the historic city centre, while Egbeda, Akinyele, Ona Ara, Lagelu, and Oluyole absorb its modern suburban growth.

name: Ogbomoso Metropolis
description: The Ogbomosho North and South LGAs forming Oyo State's second-largest urban centre, historically a major Yoruba war-era stronghold and cotton/tobacco trading town.

wikiNotes.title: Baptist mission history
wikiNotes.note: Ogbomosho became a centre of early Baptist missionary activity in Yorubaland from the 1850s, seeding some of Nigeria's oldest schools and hospitals.

name: Osogbo Metropolis
description: Osun State's capital cluster, home to the UNESCO-listed Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove on the city's edge.

wikiNotes.title: State capital creation
wikiNotes.note: Osogbo became Osun State's capital when the state was carved from Oyo State in 1991.

wikiNotes.title: Sacred grove heritage
wikiNotes.note: The Osun River sacred grove at the city's edge is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and hosts the annual Osun-Osogbo Festival.

name: Ife-Ijesa Cluster
description: The historic Ife and Ijesa LGAs of eastern Osun State - Ife regarded in Yoruba tradition as the cradle of the Yoruba people, and Ilesa as the historic Ijesa kingdom capital.

ethnicMakeup.name: Ijesa
ethnicMakeup.note: Distinct Yoruba sub-group with its own king, the Owa Obokun

wikiNotes.title: Cradle of the Yoruba
wikiNotes.note: Ile-Ife is widely regarded in Yoruba oral tradition as the origin point of the Yoruba people and the seat of the Ooni of Ife.

wikiNotes.title: Ijesa kingdom
wikiNotes.note: Ilesa was the historic capital of the Ijesa sub-group, ruled by the Owa Obokun, and a centre of the southwest gold-mining belt.

name: Akure Metropolis
description: Ondo State's capital cluster, seat of the Deji of Akure and the state's administrative and commercial hub.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Akure became Ondo State's capital in 1976 and grew rapidly around federal and state administrative functions.

name: Owo-Ose Cluster
description: The historic Owo Kingdom axis of Ondo State, known for its distinctive Yoruba-Benin hybrid art and bronze-casting tradition.

ethnicMakeup.name: Ose (Ifon and neighbouring communities)
ethnicMakeup.note: Yoruba-Edo borderland communities; verify sub-group labels locally

wikiNotes.title: Owo Kingdom art tradition
wikiNotes.note: The old Owo Kingdom produced a distinctive bronze and ivory-carving tradition blending Yoruba (Ife) and Benin artistic influences.

name: Ijebuland
description: The historic Ijebu and Remo LGAs of Ogun State, once the independent Ijebu Kingdom known for its trading networks and the Sungbo's Eredo earthworks.

ethnicMakeup.name: Remo (Ijebu-Remo)
ethnicMakeup.note: Related to Ijebu but with its own towns and identity

wikiNotes.title: Ijebu Kingdom trade power
wikiNotes.note: The pre-colonial Ijebu Kingdom, centred on Ijebu-Ode, controlled key coastal-to-interior trade routes and resisted British incursion until 1892.

wikiNotes.title: Sungbo's Eredo
wikiNotes.note: The kingdom's boundary is traced by Sungbo's Eredo, a vast earthwork wall-and-ditch system among Africa's largest ancient monuments.

name: Yewaland (Egbado)
description: The Yewa (historically Egbado) axis of western Ogun State bordering Benin Republic, home to the Yewa/Egbado Yoruba sub-group.

ethnicMakeup.name: Egun (Gun)
ethnicMakeup.note: Border communities toward Benin Republic; verify LGA spread

wikiNotes.title: Egbado-to-Yewa renaming
wikiNotes.note: The old 'Egbado' designation has increasingly been replaced locally by 'Yewa,' named for the Yewa River that runs through the area.

wikiNotes.title: Cross-border ties
wikiNotes.note: The zone's proximity to Benin Republic has shaped centuries of cross-border Yoruba-Egun trade and cultural exchange.

name: Egbaland (Abeokuta Metro)
description: Ogun State's capital cluster, historic seat of the Egba people who settled under the Olumo Rock in the 1830s.

ethnicMakeup.name: Egba (Yoruba)
ethnicMakeup.note: Ruled by the Alake of Egbaland; sub-divisions include Egba Alake, Oke-Ona and Gbagura

wikiNotes.title: Founding at Olumo Rock
wikiNotes.note: The Egba people settled at Abeokuta in 1830 under Olumo Rock, using its caves as a defensive refuge during the Yoruba civil wars.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Abeokuta became Ogun State's capital when the state was created in 1976.

name: Ado-Ekiti Metropolis
description: Ekiti State's capital cluster, seat of the Ewi of Ado-Ekiti.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Ado-Ekiti became Ekiti State's capital when the state was created from Ondo State in 1996.

name: Ilorin Metropolis
description: The three LGAs forming Ilorin, Kwara State's capital and a historic frontier emirate between Yoruba and Hausa-Fulani Nigeria.

wikiNotes.title: Fulani emirate transition
wikiNotes.note: Ilorin transitioned from a Yoruba town to a Fulani emirate in the early 19th century following the Sokoto Jihad, making it a cultural bridge city.

name: Abuja Metropolis (FCT)
description: The urbanised core area councils of the Federal Capital Territory surrounding Nigeria's purpose-built federal capital.

wikiNotes.title: Planned capital
wikiNotes.note: Abuja was purpose-built as Nigeria's federal capital starting in 1976, officially replacing Lagos in 1991, chosen partly for its central, neutral location.

name: Jos Metropolis
description: Plateau State's capital cluster on the cool Jos Plateau, built around a 20th-century tin-mining boom.

wikiNotes.title: Tin-mining boom town
wikiNotes.note: Jos grew rapidly from the early 1900s as a British colonial tin-mining hub, drawing migrant workers from across Nigeria and beyond.

wikiNotes.title: Cool highland climate
wikiNotes.note: At over 1,200m elevation, Jos has a notably cooler climate than most of Nigeria, historically marketed as a colonial hill-station retreat.

name: Lokoja / Confluence Cluster
description: Kogi State's capital area at the confluence of the Niger and Benue rivers, and the first capital of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria.

wikiNotes.title: First Northern Nigeria capital
wikiNotes.note: Lokoja was the first capital of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria, proclaimed there under Frederick Lugard in 1900.

wikiNotes.title: River confluence
wikiNotes.note: The town sits exactly at the meeting point of the Niger and Benue rivers, Nigeria's two largest waterways.

name: Makurdi Metropolis
description: Benue State's capital, on the Benue River, and the state's main administrative and trading hub.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Makurdi became Benue State's capital when the state was created in 1976.

name: Lafia-Keffi Axis
description: Nasarawa State's main administrative and historic emirate towns, close to the Abuja-Jos-Lafia corridor.

wikiNotes.title: Historic emirates
wikiNotes.note: Keffi and Lafia both trace their origins to 19th-century Fulani emirate foundations tied to the Sokoto Caliphate's southern expansion.

name: Kano Metropolis
description: The eight urban LGAs forming Kano city, one of West Africa's oldest and largest trading cities, historically ringed by ancient city walls.

wikiNotes.title: Ancient trans-Saharan hub
wikiNotes.note: Kano has been a major trans-Saharan trade centre since at least the 14th century, historically famed for leather, dyed cloth (indigo pits), and textiles.

wikiNotes.title: Kano city walls
wikiNotes.note: The old city (Kano birni) was enclosed by defensive mud walls dating to the 15th century, remnants of which still stand.

name: Kaduna Metropolis
description: Kaduna State's capital cluster, a planned colonial administrative and military city on the Kaduna River.

ethnicMakeup.name: Gbagyi (Gwari)
ethnicMakeup.note: Indigenous people of the Kaduna area

ethnicMakeup.name: Southern Kaduna groups (Kataf, Bajju, Jaba, Kagoro and others)
ethnicMakeup.note: Large migrant and resident communities, especially in Kaduna South

wikiNotes.title: Colonial planned city
wikiNotes.note: Kaduna was founded around 1913 by Frederick Lugard as the capital of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria, designed with a clear colonial urban plan.

name: Zaria Metropolis
description: The historic Zazzau emirate city and modern university town, home to Ahmadu Bello University.

wikiNotes.title: Zazzau emirate
wikiNotes.note: Zaria was the seat of the historic Zazzau (Zaria) emirate, one of the seven original Hausa city-states (Hausa Bakwai).

wikiNotes.title: University town
wikiNotes.note: Zaria became a major seat of higher education with the establishment of Ahmadu Bello University in 1962, one of Nigeria's largest universities.

name: Sokoto Metropolis
description: Sokoto State's capital, historic seat of the Sokoto Caliphate and the Sultan of Sokoto, Nigeria's foremost Islamic traditional authority.

wikiNotes.title: Caliphate seat
wikiNotes.note: Sokoto was founded around 1809 as the capital of the Sokoto Caliphate established by Usman dan Fodio, and remains the seat of the Sultanate to this day.

name: Katsina Metropolis
description: Katsina State's capital, one of the original Hausa city-states and a historic centre of Islamic scholarship.

wikiNotes.title: Hausa Bakwai city-state
wikiNotes.note: Katsina was one of the seven original Hausa city-states (Hausa Bakwai) and a major centre of Quranic scholarship before and after the Sokoto Jihad.

name: Maiduguri Metropolis
description: Borno State's capital, historic seat of the Borno Emirate and successor to the ancient Kanem-Bornu Empire.

ethnicMakeup.name: Southern Borno peoples (Babur/Bura, Marghi, Kibaku and others)

wikiNotes.title: Kanem-Bornu legacy
wikiNotes.note: Maiduguri traces its regional lineage to the centuries-old Kanem-Bornu Empire, one of Africa's longest-lived states, though the modern city was founded in 1907.

name: Yola Metropolis
description: Adamawa State's capital cluster, formed of the old Fombina/Adamawa emirate town of Yola and its modern twin Jimeta.

ethnicMakeup.name: Other Adamawa groups (Bata, Mbula, Chamba and others)

wikiNotes.title: Adamawa emirate
wikiNotes.note: Yola was founded around 1841 as the capital of the Adamawa Emirate, one of the largest emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate, spanning into modern Cameroon.

name: Bauchi Metropolis
description: Bauchi State's capital and historic emirate seat, gateway to Yankari National Park.

wikiNotes.title: Bauchi Emirate
wikiNotes.note: Bauchi was founded as an emirate seat in the early 19th century following the Sokoto Jihad, ruled by the Emir of Bauchi.

name: Gombe Metropolis
description: Gombe State's capital, a modern administrative city created as state capital in 1996.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Gombe became a state capital only in 1996 when Gombe State was carved from Bauchi State.

name: Enugu Metropolis
description: Enugu State's capital, built around early-20th-century coal mining and once capital of the old Eastern Region and briefly of Biafra.

wikiNotes.title: Coal City
wikiNotes.note: Enugu grew from a 1909 coal discovery, developing into Nigeria's first major coal-mining industrial town and giving Enugu State its 'Coal City' nickname.

wikiNotes.title: Biafran capital
wikiNotes.note: Enugu briefly served as the capital of the breakaway Republic of Biafra during the early phase of the 1967-70 Nigerian Civil War.

name: Owerri Metropolis
description: Imo State's capital cluster, known locally as the 'Eastern Heartland' and a fast-growing hospitality and events hub.

ethnicMakeup.name: Other Nigerians (Hausa, Yoruba, Ibibio and others)

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Owerri became Imo State's capital when the state was created in 1976.

name: Onitsha Metropolis
description: Anambra State's commercial powerhouse on the Niger River, home to reputedly West Africa's largest market.

wikiNotes.title: Niger River trading port
wikiNotes.note: Onitsha grew as a major 19th-century river port and colonial trading post on the east bank of the Niger, cemented by the 1965 Niger Bridge crossing.

name: Aba Metropolis
description: Abia State's commercial and light-manufacturing capital, home of the 'Aba-made' shoe and garment industry centred on Ariaria Market.

ethnicMakeup.name: Other Nigerians (Hausa, Yoruba, Ibibio and others)

wikiNotes.title: Aba-made manufacturing
wikiNotes.note: Aba's Ariaria Market area developed into Nigeria's leading hub for locally manufactured shoes, bags, and garments, collectively branded 'Aba-made.'

name: Abakaliki Metropolis
description: Ebonyi State's capital, historically known for rice cultivation and small-scale tin/lead mining.

wikiNotes.title: Rice-growing hub
wikiNotes.note: Abakaliki and its surrounding LGAs are among Nigeria's most productive rice-farming zones, giving the area a long-standing rice-trade identity.

name: Port Harcourt Metropolis
description: Rivers State's capital and Nigeria's oil-industry hub, built as a colonial coal/rail port and now the centre of the Niger Delta petroleum economy.

ethnicMakeup.name: Ikwerre
ethnicMakeup.note: Indigenous people of the Port Harcourt area

ethnicMakeup.name: Yoruba, Hausa, Ibibio, Efik and others

wikiNotes.title: Colonial coal port
wikiNotes.note: Port Harcourt was founded in 1912 as a railway terminus and export port for Enugu coal, named after colonial secretary Lewis Harcourt.

wikiNotes.title: Oil-industry centre
wikiNotes.note: The city became Nigeria's petroleum-industry hub following oil discoveries in the Niger Delta from the late 1950s, hosting major refineries and oil-company headquarters.

name: Benin City Metropolis
description: Edo State's capital, historic seat of the centuries-old Benin Kingdom and its Oba, famed for its bronze and ivory court art.

ethnicMakeup.name: Esan, Etsako and Owan
ethnicMakeup.note: Other Edo groups resident in the city

wikiNotes.title: Benin Kingdom
wikiNotes.note: Benin City was the capital of the Benin Kingdom, one of West Africa's oldest and most powerful pre-colonial states, dating back over 1,000 years.

wikiNotes.title: 1897 Punitive Expedition
wikiNotes.note: The city's royal palace and famed bronze plaques were looted by a British military expedition in 1897, a legacy still central to ongoing restitution debates.

name: Uyo Metropolis
description: Akwa Ibom State's capital cluster, a fast-growing administrative and oil-services city among the Ibibio people.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Uyo became Akwa Ibom State's capital when the state was created from Cross River State in 1987.

name: Warri Metropolis
description: Delta State's oil and commercial hub in the western Niger Delta, home to a major refinery and multi-ethnic Itsekiri-Urhobo-Ijaw population.

ethnicMakeup.name: Ijaw
ethnicMakeup.note: Gbaramatu and neighbouring Ijaw communities; claims over Warri are contested among the three groups

wikiNotes.title: Colonial trading post
wikiNotes.note: Warri developed from a historic Itsekiri Kingdom port into a major 20th-century oil-industry and trading city.

name: Asaba Metropolis
description: Delta State's capital, on the west bank of the Niger River directly opposite Onitsha, linked by the Niger Bridge.

ethnicMakeup.name: Other Nigerians (Yoruba, Hausa, Urhobo and others)

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Asaba became Delta State's capital when the state was created from Bendel State in 1991.

name: Calabar Metropolis
description: Cross River State's capital, a historic Efik trading port and one of Nigeria's oldest points of contact with European traders.

wikiNotes.title: Historic trading port
wikiNotes.note: Calabar (Old Calabar) was a major Atlantic-era Efik trading port from the 17th century onward, later a British colonial administrative centre.

name: Lagos Metropolis
description: The sixteen metropolitan LGAs of Lagos State, Nigeria's largest city and commercial capital, built around the historic Eko settlement on Lagos Island and its lagoon-side mainland.

ethnicMakeup.name: Yoruba (Eko, Awori and other Yoruba groups)
ethnicMakeup.note: Eko and Awori are the indigenous Yoruba communities

ethnicMakeup.name: Edo, Urhobo, Ijaw, Itsekiri, Ibibio-Efik and others
Aguda and Saro (Afro-Brazilian and Sierra Leonean returnee descendants)

wikiNotes.title: Sixteen metropolitan LGAs
wikiNotes.note: Lagos State officially classes 16 of its 20 LGAs as metropolitan; Badagry, Epe, Ibeju-Lekki and Ikorodu are non-metropolitan.

wikiNotes.title: Nigeria's most cosmopolitan city
wikiNotes.note: Indigenous Yoruba communities live alongside some of Nigeria's largest Igbo, Hausa-Fulani and minority-group populations, making Lagos the country's most ethnically mixed city.

name: Yenagoa Metropolis
description: Bayelsa State's capital on the Ekole Creek in the heart of the Niger Delta, home to the Epie-Atissa and surrounding Ijaw communities.

ethnicMakeup.name: Other Nigerians (Igbo, Yoruba, Hausa and others)

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Yenagoa became the capital when Bayelsa State was created from Rivers State in 1996.

name: Dutse Metropolis
description: Jigawa State's capital, seat of the Dutse Emirate, created as a state capital when Jigawa was carved from Kano State in 1991.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Dutse became the capital when Jigawa State was created from Kano State in 1991.

name: Birnin Kebbi Metropolis
description: Kebbi State's capital area on the Rima River, centre of the historic Kebbi Kingdom.

wikiNotes.title: Kebbi Kingdom centre
wikiNotes.note: Birnin Kebbi is the capital of Kebbi State (created 1991) and lies in the heartland of the historic Kebbi Kingdom.

name: Minna Metropolis
description: Niger State's capital cluster on Gbagyi (Gwari) ancestral land, a railway and administrative town near the Shiroro and Kainji power corridor.

ethnicMakeup.name: Gbagyi (Gwari)
ethnicMakeup.note: Indigenous people of the Minna area

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Minna has been the capital of Niger State since the state was created in 1976.

name: Jalingo Metropolis
description: Taraba State's capital, created when Taraba was carved from Gongola State in 1991, at the meeting point of Fulani, Mumuye, Jukun and Hausa communities.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Jalingo became the capital when Taraba State was created from Gongola State in 1991.

name: Damaturu Metropolis
description: Yobe State's capital on the Maiduguri-Kano corridor, created as a state capital when Yobe was carved from Borno State in 1991.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Damaturu became the capital when Yobe State was created from Borno State in 1991.

name: Gusau Metropolis
description: Zamfara State's capital, a Hausa trading and grain-marketing town created as a state capital when Zamfara was carved from Sokoto State in 1996.

wikiNotes.title: State capital
wikiNotes.note: Gusau became the capital when Zamfara State was created from Sokoto State in 1996.

name: Eko (Lagos Island and Mainland)
description: Historic core of Lagos: the Eko settlement, seat of the Oba of Lagos and the Idejo (White Cap) chieftaincy, with Awori and returnee-descended communities.

ethnicMakeup.name: Aguda and Saro
ethnicMakeup.note: Afro-Brazilian and Sierra Leonean returnee descendants

name: Awori
description: Awori Yoruba sub-group of Lagos and south-western Ogun, indigenous to much of the Lagos mainland and Ota.

name: Egun (Badagry)
description: Egun (Gun/Ogu) coastal people of Badagry, a community that continues across the border into Benin Republic; Badagry was a major slave-trade port.

wikiNotes.title: Egun (Badagry)
wikiNotes.note: Home of the Egun Zangbeto night-guardian masquerades.

name: Lagos Ijebu (Ikorodu, Epe, Ibeju-Lekki)
description: Ijebu-related lagoon-side communities in the eastern non-metropolitan part of Lagos State; Awori communities are also present in Ibeju-Lekki.

name: Oyo (Alaafin's Kingdom)
description: Heartland of the historic Oyo Empire around present-day Oyo town, seat of the Alaafin of Oyo.

name: Oke-Ogun
description: The savanna plain of north-western Oyo State, home to Oyo-Yoruba communities such as Saki, Igboho and Iseyin, the last known for Aso-Oke weaving.

name: Ibarapa
description: The Ibarapa Yoruba towns (Igboora, Igangan, Tapa and neighbours) on the western edge of Oyo State.

name: Iwo-Ede-Ejigbo axis
description: Oyo-Yoruba towns of north-western Osun State, including the seats of the Oluwo of Iwo, the Timi of Ede and the Olojigbo of Ejigbo.

name: Akoko
description: Hill-country Yoruba sub-group of north-eastern Ondo State organised in many small kingdoms (Ikare, Oka, Ikaram and others).

wikiNotes.title: Akoko
wikiNotes.note: Hosts the Ariginya (local wrestling) festival at Ikare-Akoko.

name: Ilaje
description: Riverine and coastal Yoruba sub-group of southern Ondo State, fishing and oil-region communities of the Atlantic coast.

wikiNotes.title: Ilaje
wikiNotes.note: Shares the Biripo musical tradition with the Apoi and the Ikale.

name: Ikale
description: Yoruba sub-group of southern Ondo State centred on Okitipupa and Irele, in Ikaleland.

wikiNotes.title: Ikale
wikiNotes.note: Shares the Biripo musical tradition with the Ilaje and Apoi; also known for the Irokute festival at Okitipupa.

name: Ondo Kingdom and neighbours
description: Yoruba communities around the Ondo Kingdom under the Osemawe of Ondo and Ile-Oluji.

name: Ekiti Yoruba
description: The whole of Ekiti State, homeland of the Ekiti sub-group of the Yoruba, organised in some sixteen historic kingdoms each with its own crowned Oba.

name: Igbomina and Ekiti (Kwara)
description: Igbomina and Ekiti-Yoruba communities of southern Kwara State.

name: Nupe (Kwara)
description: Nupe communities along the Niger River in northern Kwara State, seat of the Etsu Patigi.

name: Baruba (Borgu, Kwara)
description: Baruba (Bariba/Baatonu) and related Borgu communities in the north-west of Kwara State, continuous with the Borgu region of Benin Republic.

name: FCT indigenous peoples
description: The original inhabitants of the Federal Capital Territory, who lived in the area long before Abuja was built.

wikiNotes.title: FCT indigenous peoples
wikiNotes.note: Indigenous groups are recognised through area-council traditional rulers such as the Ona of Abaji.

name: Berom
description: Largest indigenous people of the Jos Plateau, centred on Jos South, Barkin Ladi and Riyom under the Gbong Gwom Jos.

wikiNotes.title: Berom
wikiNotes.note: Their festivals were merged into the annual Nzem Berom cultural festival held around April.

name: Ngas and Mwaghavul (central Plateau)
description: Ngas (Pankshin, Kanke) and Mwaghavul (Mangu, Bokkos) communities of the central Plateau highlands.

name: Southern Plateau (Tarok, Goemai, Pan, Mupun)
description: Tarok (Langtang), Goemai (Shendam), Pan (Qua'an Pan) and related communities of the southern Plateau lowlands.

name: Igala
description: Eastern Kogi kingdom centred on Idah, seat of the Attah Igala.

wikiNotes.title: Igala
wikiNotes.note: Idah hosts the Ocho hunting festival, banned in 1963 and revived in 2018.

name: Ebira
description: Ebira (Igbira) heartland of central Kogi around Okene, under the Ohinoyi of Ebiraland; Ogori and Magongo communities have distinct local traditions.

name: Okun Yoruba
description: Yoruba-speaking Okun communities (Kabba, Ijumu, Yagba, Mopa) of western Kogi.

ethnicMakeup.name: Okun Yoruba (Owe, Bunu, Yagba, Ijumu, Iyagba)

name: Tiv
description: Tiv heartland of Benue State under the Tor Tiv; the Tiv also live in Nasarawa, Taraba and Plateau states.

wikiNotes.title: Tiv
wikiNotes.note: Home of the Kwagh-hir theatrical tradition, inscribed by UNESCO in 2019.

name: Idoma
description: Idoma communities of southern Benue State around Otukpo, seat of the Och'Idoma.

wikiNotes.title: Idoma
wikiNotes.note: Home of the Eje Alekwu ancestral festival.

name: Igede
description: Igede-speaking communities of Oju and Obi in south-eastern Benue State.

wikiNotes.title: Igede
wikiNotes.note: Known for the Ige-Agba new yam festival.

name: Eggon
description: Eggon communities of northern Nasarawa State, under the Aren Eggon.

name: Alago (Arago) and neighbours
description: Alago, Migili and related communities of southern Nasarawa State, including the Doma chiefdom under the Osana of Doma.

name: Nupe (Niger State)
description: Nupe kingdom of central Niger State centred on Bida, seat of the Etsu Nupe.

wikiNotes.title: Nupe (Niger State)
wikiNotes.note: Bida is known for brasswork and glass-bead making.

name: Gbagyi (Gwari) of Niger State
description: Gbagyi (Gwari) communities of eastern Niger State, including the Minna area.

name: Borgu and Kambari
description: Kambari, Bokobaru and other communities of north-western Niger State along the Benin Republic border.

name: Southern Kaduna peoples
description: The highland peoples of southern Kaduna State, including Kataf (Atyap), Bajju, Ham (Jaba), Kagoro (Gworok), Fantswam, Ikulu, Adara and Kurama.

wikiNotes.title: Southern Kaduna peoples
wikiNotes.note: The Nok terracotta culture is named after Nok village in Jaba LGA; the Afan festival is held at Kagoro on 1 January.

name: Daura Emirate
description: Hausa communities of northern Katsina State around Daura, regarded in tradition as the ancestral home of the Hausa.

wikiNotes.title: Daura Emirate
wikiNotes.note: Daura is tied to the Bayajidda legend of Hausa origins.

name: Zuru (Dakarkari)
description: The Dakarkari and related peoples of the Zuru Emirate in southern Kebbi State.

name: Yauri Emirate
description: The Yauri Emirate on the Niger River in south-western Kebbi State, home of the Reshe, Gungawa and related river peoples.

name: Argungu (Kebbawa)
description: The Kebbawa communities of the Argungu Emirate, historic heart of the Kebbi Kingdom.

wikiNotes.title: Argungu (Kebbawa)
wikiNotes.note: Host of the Argungu Fishing Festival.

name: Hadejia Emirate
description: Hausa communities of the Hadejia Emirate on the Hadejia-Jama'are floodplain of Jigawa State.

name: Kanuri heartland
description: Core Kanuri-speaking LGAs of Borno State, successors of the Kanem-Bornu Empire and the Shehu of Borno's domain.

name: Bura (Babur) and Biu
description: The Bura (Babur) and related communities of the Biu plateau in southern Borno State, under the Mai of Biu.

name: Marghi, Kibaku and Gwoza hill peoples
description: Marghi, Kibaku (Chibok) and Gwoza hill peoples of southern Borno State.

name: Bachama (Bwatiye)
description: Bachama (Bwatiye) communities of the Benue valley in southern Adamawa State, under the Hama Bachama.

name: Northern Adamawa highland peoples
description: Kamwe (Higi), Kilba, Fali, Margi and neighbouring peoples of the Mandara-foothill north of Adamawa State.

wikiNotes.title: Northern Adamawa highland peoples
wikiNotes.note: The Sukur Cultural Landscape lies in Madagali LGA.

name: Jukun (Wukari Federation)
description: Jukun communities of southern Taraba State under the Aku Uka of Wukari, successors of the Kwararafa confederacy.

wikiNotes.title: Jukun (Wukari Federation)
wikiNotes.note: Ibi hosts the Nwonyo International Fishing and Cultural Festival.

name: Kuteb and Ichen (Takum)
description: Kuteb, Ichen and related communities of Takum and Ussa in south-eastern Taraba State.

name: Mumuye
description: Mumuye communities of central Taraba State, renowned for their figurative wood sculpture.

name: Mambilla
description: Mambilla Plateau communities of Taraba State along the Cameroon border.

name: Sayawa (Zaar)
description: Sayawa (Zaar) communities of southern Bauchi State.

name: Tangale and Waja
description: Tangale (Billiri, Kaltungo) and Waja (Balanga, Shongom) communities of southern Gombe State.

name: Fika Emirate
description: The Fika Emirate of southern Yobe State, under the Mai of Fika, home of the Bolewa, Ngizim and Karekare.

name: Ohafia, Arochukwu and Abam
description: Igbo communities of north-eastern Abia State: the Aro of Arochukwu, the Ohafia warrior tradition and the Abam.

name: Ngwa and Ukwa
description: Ngwa and Ukwa Igbo communities of southern Abia State, hinterland of the Aba commercial centre.

name: Ibeku and Umuahia axis
description: Igbo communities of central and northern Abia around Umuahia (Ibeku), including Ikwuano and Isuikwuato.

name: Mbaise
description: The three Mbaise LGAs of Imo State, a densely populated Igbo cultural area.

name: Orlu area
description: Igbo communities of the Orlu area of Imo State, including Nkwerre and Ideato, home of Arondizuogu.

wikiNotes.title: Orlu area
wikiNotes.note: Arondizuogu in Ideato North hosts the Ikeji masquerade festival.

name: Okigwe area
description: Igbo communities of northern Imo State around Okigwe.

name: Oguta and Egbema
description: Igbo communities of the Oguta Lake area and the Egbema oil belt in south-western Imo State.

name: Nri-Awka heartland
description: The Nri and Awka heartland of Anambra State, associated with the ritual Nri Kingdom and Awka's metalworking tradition.

wikiNotes.title: Nri-Awka heartland
wikiNotes.note: The Eze Nri holds a ritual kingship associated with the Nri Kingdom.

name: Anambra River basin
description: River-basin communities of northern Anambra State, including Aguleri and Umueri; Anambra West has strong Igala links.

name: Nnewi, Aguata and Orumba
description: Igbo communities of southern Anambra State, home of Nnewi's industrial cluster.

name: Nsukka Igbo
description: The Igbo communities of northern Enugu State, centred on Nsukka.

name: Nkanu
description: Nkanu Igbo communities south of Enugu.

name: Udi, Awgu and Oji River area
description: Igbo communities of the western Enugu escarpment, including the Ngwo clan associated with the Odo festival.

ethnicMakeup.name: Igbo (Udi, Awgu, Ezeagu, Oji River, Aninri)

name: Afikpo (Ehugbo)
description: The Afikpo (Ehugbo) Igbo of southern Ebonyi State, known for elaborate masquerade traditions.

name: Ezza, Izzi and Ikwo
description: Northern Ebonyi Igbo communities around Abakaliki, including Izzi, Ezza and Ikwo.

name: Ivo, Ohaozara and Onicha
description: Igbo communities of south-western Ebonyi State, including the Uburu and Okposi salt-lake areas.

name: Ikwerre
description: Ikwerre communities, indigenous to Port Harcourt and Obio-Akpor and to the Ikwerre and Emohua areas.

name: Ogoni
description: The four Ogoni-linked LGAs of south-eastern Rivers State.

ethnicMakeup.name: Eleme
ethnicMakeup.note: Distinct language, usually counted with Ogoniland

name: Eastern Ijaw and Degema (Kalabari, Okrika, Bonny, Opobo)
description: Eastern Ijaw kingdoms of the Rivers creeks, including Kalabari, Okrika, Bonny and Opobo, plus the Degema.

wikiNotes.title: Eastern Ijaw and Degema (Kalabari, Okrika, Bonny, Opobo)
wikiNotes.note: The Ekine (Sekiapu) masquerade society is central to Kalabari culture.

name: Etche, Ekpeye, Ogba and Omuma
description: Igbo-related communities of northern and central Rivers State.

name: Obolo (Andoni)
description: Obolo (Andoni) communities across the Rivers/Akwa Ibom coast.

name: Ijaw of Bayelsa
description: The Ijaw (Izon) clans of Bayelsa State, with Epie-Atissa in Yenagoa.

wikiNotes.title: Ijaw of Bayelsa
wikiNotes.note: Nembe (Brass) was a major palm-oil trading kingdom.

name: Ogbia
description: The Ogbia people of Bayelsa State, in whose area Oloibiri lies.

wikiNotes.title: Ogbia
wikiNotes.note: Oloibiri saw Nigeria's first commercial oil discovery in 1956.

name: Ibibio
description: Ibibio communities, the largest group in Akwa Ibom State.

name: Annang
description: Annang communities of north-western Akwa Ibom State, closely related to the Ibibio.

name: Oron
description: Oron communities of the south-eastern Akwa Ibom coast.

name: Eket and Ibeno
description: Eket and Ibeno communities of the south-western Akwa Ibom coast and its oil-industry belt.

name: Efik and Calabar area
description: Efik and related communities of the Calabar estuary, an Atlantic trading society governed through the Ekpe society.

name: Ekoi (Ejagham)
description: Ekoi (Ejagham) communities of the central Cross River forest belt, including the Ikom monolith area.

name: Yakurr, Abi and Biase
description: Yakö (Yakurr), Abi and Biase communities of southern-central Cross River State.

wikiNotes.title: Yakurr, Abi and Biase
wikiNotes.note: Ugep in Yakurr hosts the Leboku new yam festival.

name: Northern Cross River (Ogoja, Bekwarra, Boki, Yala, Obudu)
description: Boki, Bekwarra, Yala, Bette and Ogoja communities of northern Cross River State.

name: Itsekiri
description: The Itsekiri Kingdom of the western Niger Delta under the Olu of Warri, with Ode-Itsekiri as its cradle.

ethnicMakeup.name: Ijaw and Urhobo
ethnicMakeup.note: Mixed communities; local claims are contested

wikiNotes.title: Itsekiri
wikiNotes.note: Itsekiri identity centres on the Olu of Warri, who marks his coronation anniversary each August.

name: Urhobo
description: Urhobo kingdoms of the central Delta State.

ethnicMakeup.name: Okpe
ethnicMakeup.note: Closely related to Urhobo, with its own traditional ruler

name: Isoko
description: Isoko communities of southern Delta State.

name: Ijaw of Delta
description: Ijaw communities of the Delta creeks, including the Gbaramatu Kingdom in Warri South West.

wikiNotes.title: Ijaw of Delta
wikiNotes.note: Gbaramatu Kingdom hosts the seven-day Amaseikumor festival.

name: Anioma (Delta Igbo)
description: Igbo-speaking communities of Delta North, often grouped as Anioma, west of the Niger.

name: Ukwuani (Kwale)
description: The Ukwuani (Kwale) people of southern Delta North, whose language is close to but distinct from Igbo.

name: Edo (Bini) heartland
description: Edo (Bini) heartland of southern Edo State, home of the Benin Kingdom and its Oba.

name: Esan
description: Esan communities of central Edo State, whose rulers bear the title Onojie.

name: Afemai (Etsako, Owan and Akoko-Edo)
description: The northern Edo peoples, called Afemai, including Etsako, Owan and Akoko-Edo communities.

ethnicMakeup.name: Akoko-Edo
ethnicMakeup.note: Distinct Edoid-speaking communities, not to be confused with Akoko in Ondo State
